h1: The 6 Best Snow Blowers Under $500 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Snow Blowers Under $500: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six electric snow blowers under $500, from corded 22-inch machines to 40V and 48V cordless, scored for clearing power and fit.
summary: Under $500 you are shopping electric, and the first decision is cord or battery. The Westinghouse WSnow22 is the top pick for a driveway near an outlet, the ETOOLAB 40V is the best cordless for deeper snow, and the EWORK throws the farthest of the battery models. Skip the smallest machines if your driveway holds more than one car.
intro: The most expensive mistake in this price range is buying for the snowfall you hope for instead of the one you get. An electric blower with a 10 in intake chokes on a plow ridge left at the curb, and a cordless pack that clears a short walk in one pass may quit halfway down a long drive. Width and depth of the intake, not horsepower claims, decide whether you finish in one outing.

We ranked six electric models that sit under $500, three corded and three cordless, using the published specs: clearing path, intake depth, rated snow moved, throw distance, lighting and battery setup. Each one is scored on the Primea framework and placed against its neighbours, so you can see exactly what you give up when you move down a rank.

products.name: Westinghouse WSnow22 Corded Snow Blower
products.verdict: The widest, deepest intake in the group, with no battery to run flat.
products.description:
The WSnow22 opens a 22 in wide by 13 in deep path and is rated at 840 lb of snow per minute from a 120V, 15A corded motor. A rubber-tipped steel auger, dual LED lights, 7 inch wheels and a 180 degree chute round out the package.

It tops the list because corded power does not fade as it works. The 13 in intake also lifts it above the 10 in Westinghouse WSnow20, which handles the same plow-ridge snow in more passes. The Snow Joe SJ627E posts the same path and throughput on paper, so this one wins on auger and wheel details.

Buy it for a two-car driveway or a long walk within reach of an outlet. The caveat is the cord itself: you will be steering around it, and a 15A tool needs a heavy outdoor extension to avoid voltage drop.
cons: Cord limits where you can work
products.idealFor: Two-car driveways and long walks that sit near an exterior outlet.
products.skipIf: Your clearing area is far from power and you cannot manage a cord.

products.name: ETOOLAB 40V Cordless Snow Blower 20 in
products.verdict: Cordless freedom with a 12 in intake that handles real depth.
products.description:
The ETOOLAB pairs a 20 in clearing width with a 12 in intake depth, driven by a 2500 RPM brushless motor and two 20V 4.0Ah packs. The listing quotes up to 25 ft of throw, which is enough to clear the snow off a short drive in one lane.

It ranks second because the intake depth beats both the EWORK and the VOLTASK on paper, where those two publish only the width. Brushless motors also run cooler and wear less than brushed ones, so this keeps its power late in a pack. It gives up to the WSnow22 on sheer runtime, since two 4.0Ah packs only go so far.

Buy it for a short driveway plus walkways. The caveat is battery capacity: a long drive after a heavy storm will drain both packs, and the listing does not publish a runtime figure.
cons: Runtime depends on two small packs
products.idealFor: Short driveways and walkways where a cord would be a nuisance.
products.skipIf: You face long drives or wet, heavy snow that drains packs.

products.name: Snow Joe SJ627E Corded Electric Snow Blower
products.verdict: Matches the WSnow22 on the spec sheet and trails only on detail.
products.description:
The SJ627E clears a 22 in by 13 in path with a 15 amp corded motor and is rated up to 840 lb of snow moved. Two 1.5W LED lights and a 180 degree rotating chute are part of the build.

Its numbers match the Westinghouse WSnow22 almost line for line, which is why it lands one rung down rather than far below. The listing does not call out the auger material or the wheel size, and the LED lights are rated at only 1.5W each, so the tiebreak goes to the model that documents more.

Buy it if you prefer a name you recognise and want the same big path as the leader. The caveat is the same cord tradeoff, plus a less detailed spec listing, so confirm the wheel and auger details before you commit.
products.idealFor: Mid-sized driveways near a garage outlet.
products.skipIf: You want documented auger and wheel construction before buying.

products.name: EWORK 40V Cordless Snow Blower 20 in
products.verdict: Throws farther than any other battery model in the ranking.
products.description:
The EWORK clears a 20 in swath and claims up to 30 ft of throw, the longest of the three cordless picks here. It runs on two 20V 4Ah packs, the charger is included, and the chute adjusts for direction.

It sits below the ETOOLAB because the listing publishes no intake depth and no motor type, so you cannot judge how it handles a plow ridge. The throw advantage is real for a narrow lawn or fence line, where the farther the snow lands the less you re-clear later.

Buy it if you have a narrow strip to clear and want a ready-to-run kit. The caveat is that the same two 4Ah packs power a 20 in path, so wet snow will shorten the run, and a missing depth figure means you should assume lighter, shallower snowfalls.
products.idealFor: Narrow lawns and fence lines where throw distance matters.
products.skipIf: You regularly get deep drifts that need a published intake figure.

products.name: VOLTASK 48V Cordless Snow Blower 20 in
products.verdict: Higher voltage and built-in lights, but the least data to go on.
products.description:
The VOLTASK is a 48V system made from two 24V packs, with a 20 in brushless path, dual LED lights, smooth wheels and an ergonomic handle. Higher system voltage lets a motor draw less current for the same power, which tends to help sustained work.

It ranks fifth because the listing never states the intake depth, the throw distance or the pack capacity, so the advantage of 48V cannot be confirmed against the 40V pair above it. The built-in lights are the clearest practical edge, useful when you clear before work or after dark.

Buy it if your snow comes early or late in the day and you want lights without a headlamp. The caveat is the thin spec sheet: without a capacity or throw figure, you are buying on voltage alone.
products.idealFor: Dawn and dusk clearing where built-in lights help.
products.skipIf: You need published throw and capacity figures to size the job.

products.name: Westinghouse WSnow20 Corded Snow Blower
products.verdict: The cheapest way into corded clearing, sized for small jobs.
products.description:
The WSnow20 is a 120V, 15A, 1800W corded machine with a 20 in by 10 in path, rated at 680 lb per minute and a 25 ft throw. Its rubber-tipped steel auger rides on 7 inch wheels.

It lands last because the 10 in intake is three inches shallower than the WSnow22, and the 680 lb per minute rating trails the 840 of the two 22 in models. That gap shows up as extra passes whenever the plow leaves a ridge. It costs far less, which is why it is still on the list.

Buy it for a small driveway or a short walk near an outlet. The caveat is capacity: a long double-width drive turns this into a tiring job, and it has no listed lights, so it suits daylight clearing.
products.idealFor: Small driveways and short walks near an outlet.
products.skipIf: You clear a two-car drive or want built-in lighting.

methodology.title: Clearing capacity
methodology.description: We weighed path width, intake depth and rated snow moved per minute, because they set how many passes a job takes.

methodology.title: Power source
methodology.description: Corded and battery machines trade endless runtime against freedom from a cord, so we judged each against its likely job size.

methodology.title: Throw and chute control
methodology.description: Published throw distance and chute rotation decide where the snow lands and how often you re-clear.

methodology.title: Build and drive
methodology.description: Auger material, wheel size and motor type were weighed for how well each holds up and rolls over uneven pavement.

methodology.title: Value under $500
methodology.description: We compared how much documented capability each model delivers for its price bucket, with cost and spec gaps weighed together.

whatMatters.detail: Intake depth is how tall a bank of snow the machine can swallow. It matters because a plow ridge or a 10 inch fall can exceed a shallow intake and force you to shave the pile in layers. On a listing, look for a stated depth figure; the 13 in models here beat the 10 in WSnow20.

A corded blower delivers constant power but ties you to a cord and an outlet. A cordless unit moves freely but is limited by pack capacity. Check the drive length against the outlet distance, and for battery models look for amp-hour ratings, since two 4.0Ah packs only cover a short job.

Width is the swath you clear per pass. A 22 in path finishes a double-width driveway in fewer lanes than a 20 in one, and every extra lane adds time. Compare the published width, and remember that wider machines are heavier to turn at the end of each row.

Throw distance is how far the chute launches snow, and it decides whether you re-clear the same spot. Shorter throws pile snow along the edge you just cleared. Look for a stated range, such as the 30 ft claimed by the EWORK, and treat it as a best-case figure.

Built-in lights matter because most snow gets cleared before sunrise or after dark. Without lights you work blind to ice patches and edges. Check the listing for LED lights; the Westinghouse WSnow22, Snow Joe SJ627E and VOLTASK all list them, while the WSnow20 does not.

howToChoose.intro: The first decision is whether you can tolerate a cord or need battery freedom. Match this to the distance from your outlet and the length of your drive.

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: Constant power with no runtime limit, but the cord limits reach. The Westinghouse WSnow22 and Snow Joe SJ627E suit drives near an outlet.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: Move anywhere without a cord, at the cost of finite pack runtime. The ETOOLAB 40V and EWORK 40V suit short drives and walks.

howToChoose.note: Choose corded for anything longer than one car, and cordless only when the outlet is far away.

faq.q: Can an electric snow blower handle wet, heavy snow?
faq.a: Corded models like the Westinghouse WSnow22 keep steady power through heavy snow, while cordless picks such as the ETOOLAB drain two 4.0Ah packs faster. Take shallower passes in wet snow, and expect all of these to struggle more than a gas two-stage.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake buyers make?
faq.a: Buying a 20 in cordless for a long driveway. The ETOOLAB and EWORK each run on two small packs, so a double-width drive can outlast them. Match pack capacity to the longest job you face, or choose the corded WSnow22.

faq.q: Is the Snow Joe SJ627E worth it over the WSnow22?
faq.a: They share a 22 in by 13 in path and a rated 840 lb of snow moved. Pick the SJ627E if you prefer the brand and the price is lower, and pick the WSnow22 for its documented steel auger and 7 inch wheels.

faq.q: How do I set up a corded blower safely?
faq.a: Use an outdoor-rated extension cord sized for 15A, and plug into a GFCI outlet. Keep the cord behind you as you work, as with the WSnow20 and WSnow22, so the auger never rolls over it.

faq.q: How should I maintain a cordless snow blower?
faq.a: Store the packs indoors, since cold reduces capacity, and charge them before the season. On the VOLTASK 48V and ETOOLAB, clear packed snow from the chute and auger after use so ice does not bind the motor next time.

faq.q: Do any of these work on gravel driveways?
faq.a: Gravel is a risk for all of them, because augers can throw stones. The rubber-tipped steel auger on the WSnow20 and WSnow22 reduces surface scuffing on pavement, but none of these are built for loose gravel, so keep the intake slightly above the surface.

finalTake: Buy the Westinghouse WSnow22 if you have an outlet within reach, because its 22 in by 13 in path is the best clearing power in this price range. Choose the ETOOLAB 40V when a cord is impossible and your snow is moderate. Take the Westinghouse WSnow20 for small walks on a tight budget. Treat any battery blower as a short-drive tool, not a storm machine.
